Image Source.d: Drag a photo, PNG, JPEG, TIFF, or BMP straight from Finder onto the canvas and it becomes a live texture. This is the simplest way to get your own artwork, logo, or photography into a patch.

Slideshow.d: Steps through a folder of images on a beat interval, with an optional crossfade between them. Point it at a folder and it becomes a self-running photo reel locked to the tempo.

Shape.d: Draws crisp, perfectly smooth vector shapes out of pure math, 20 primitives from simple circles and stars to hearts, gears, and blobs, no pixelation no matter how big you scale them.

Formula.d: A shader playground with more than two dozen ready-made looks baked in, plasma fields, Mandelbrot and Julia fractals, Truchet tiles, Voronoi cells, phyllotaxis spirals, each with four knobs you can wire up to anything else in the patch.

Field Pixel.d: Runs your kernel once per pixel, compiled straight to a real GPU shader, an image generator or effect you write from scratch instead of picking off a shelf.

Text.d: Renders crisp type using any font installed on your Mac via CoreText, titles, lyrics, captions. Alignment, size, and letter spacing are all adjustable live.

Video.d: Plays back any movie file as a live texture, with a Loop switch and a speed dial, crank speed negative and it plays backwards. The simplest way to get found footage moving inside a patch.

Video In.d: Captures a live feed straight from your Mac's camera, the built-in FaceTime HD camera, an external USB webcam, or a Continuity Camera iPhone, with a device picker, a resolution choice, and a mirror toggle for when a front-facing camera reads reversed.

Syphon In.d: Pulls a live video feed straight out of another app publishing over the macOS Syphon protocol, OBS, Resolume, TouchDesigner, with no re-encoding.

NDI In.d: Receives any NDI video source on the network as an image. Pick it from the list, which rescans in the background. Video only. Needs the free NDI runtime from ndi.video.

Noise.d: Generates organic, ever-shifting texture, soft clouds, ridged terrain, cell-like Voronoi and Worley patterns, or plain white static, from six procedural noise algorithms.

Texture.d: A pattern factory with ten procedural surfaces on tap, bricks, cell clusters, swirling marble, wood grain, wave bands, checkers, clouds, and rocky Musgrave terrain, all generated live rather than loaded from a file, so they can be animated forever.

Ramp.d: A clean two-color gradient, linear, radial, angular, diamond, or spiral. Perfect as a soft backdrop, a mask, or a blend driver for another effect.

Geometry.d: A deep library of 3D building blocks, cube, sphere, icosphere, cylinder, cone, torus, plane, disc, and more exotic forms like torus knots and Möbius strips, with adjustable tessellation so they stay smooth up close.

Model 3D.d: Imports your own 3D models, OBJ, PLY, STL, or USD/USDZ, with automatic centering and scale normalization, so anything exported from Blender or elsewhere just drops in and works. (glTF and FBX aren't supported yet.)

Text 3D.d: Takes the same lettering and extrudes it into a real, beveled 3D mesh you can light, rotate, and shade like any other object in the scene, logo stings and title cards with actual depth.

Null 3D.d: A pure pass-through for a geometry cable, forwards the mesh, material, and mapping from its single input unchanged. Exists purely to route or organize a 3D chain, the geometry equivalent of the plain Null node.

Ocean.d: Ocean is a 3D node: it builds, changes or lights geometry that Render 3D turns into a picture. It takes picture in and gives 3D shape out. Its controls include resolution, size, amplitude, wavelength.

Material.d: Overrides the surface material of whatever geometry passes through it, so one authored look can be shared by several shapes.

Displacement.d: Physically pushes a mesh's vertices using a texture, real 3D geometry displacement, distinct from the 2D Displace/Liquify image filters, which only warp a flat image and never move actual geometry.

Audio Displacement.d: Deforms a mesh in real time from live audio, with five modes: waveform push, FFT-spectrum warp, concentric ripples, Chladni-plate standing-wave patterns, or a straight axis push.

Audio Ribbon.d: Builds its own ribbon-shaped mesh directly from an audio signal, no upstream geometry needed. Width, height scale, segment count, gain, and smoothing are all adjustable, alongside its own transform and material.

Mapping.d: Changes how a material's texture maps are looked up on a surface without altering the mesh itself, UV, Generated, or Object coordinate space, plus per-axis offset, rotation, scale, and a triplanar-blend control.

Particle System.d: Spawns and simulates a stream of moving points with adjustable emit rate, lifetime, initial speed, and turbulence, sparks, dust, snow, or drifting motes, all reacting in real time.

Cloth.d: Cloth is a 3D node: it builds, changes or lights geometry that Render 3D turns into a picture. It takes 3D shape in and gives 3D shape out. Its controls include pinned, stiffness, iterations, damping.

Join Geometry.d: Merges up to four geometry inputs into a single mesh, using plain concatenation or real CSG Union/Intersect/Difference. Each input's own transform is baked in before combining.

Metaballs.d: Generates blobs that smoothly merge into one another rather than intersecting with hard edges, surfaced via marching cubes over a summed field of up to 8 balls.

Resynthesize 3D.d: The 3D counterpart to the image Resynth node, each generation mutates the previous generation, not the original input, so the mesh drifts progressively over time via displace, jitter, smooth, twist, bulge, extrude, subdivide, and squash operators.

Image to Points.d: Converts an image into a point cloud, one particle per sampled pixel on a density grid, with brightness pushing each point out of a flat plane by a depth amount, and darker pixels dropped entirely so a cutout image reads as a shape.

Depth Projection.d: Turns a depth map, plus an optional colour image, into a 3D point cloud or a triangulated surface. It supports pinhole camera, planar, radial and cylindrical projections, depth curves, and edge tearing.

Curve.d: Generates a spline that works two ways: as visible tube geometry (adjustable radius, sides, taper) and as a path other nodes can follow.

Instance on Points.d: Stamps a copy of one mesh onto the points of another, turning a single object into a scattered crowd drawn as GPU instances, one draw call for thousands of copies.

Set Vertex Color.d: Writes colour onto each element: vertex colour on a mesh, or per-particle colour on a point cloud, whichever the input carries.

Wrap.d: Conforms one mesh onto the surface of another, every source vertex moves to the nearest point on the target's surface, real shrinkwrap-style deformation.

Field Modifier.d: Runs your kernel once per vertex of an incoming mesh, letting you rewrite position, normal, color, or any custom attribute with plain math instead of picking from a fixed deformer list.

Field Primitive.d: A pure generator: builds 3D point geometry entirely from your kernel, starting from a topology scaffold, points, a plane, a sphere, a torus, that your code then reshapes.

Distribute Points on Faces.d: Scatters points evenly across the surface area of an input mesh (area-weighted, not vertex-based) so coverage stays uniform even on meshes with uneven face sizes.

Points to Vertices.d: Converts an incoming point cloud into a bare mesh made only of vertices, no edges, no faces, so cloud data can re- enter mesh-only operators like Merge by Distance.

Distribute Points in Grid.d: Generates a plain rectangular lattice of points from scratch, no geometry input needed, with adjustable count, spacing, jitter, and per-point size.

Merge by Distance.d: Welds vertices that lie within a threshold distance of each other, the cleanup pass that closes seams left behind by a scatter or conversion node, or, cranked up, collapses geometry together outright.

Switcher 3D.d: Cycles between up to four connected 3D geometry inputs, forwarding whichever is currently active rather than blending them, a hard cut, timed by beats/seconds or set manually.

Camera.d: Defines the viewpoint for Render 3D, perspective or orthographic, field of view, distance/azimuth/elevation orbit around a target, roll, and clip planes.

Light.d: Defines a single light source for Render 3D, Directional, Point, Sun, Ambient, or Spot, with azimuth/elevation/distance placement, color, intensity, falloff, and cone angle/softness for spots.

HDRI.d: Loads an equirectangular HDR/EXR image and hands it to Render 3D as a real image-based environment, replacing the built-in sky gradient.

Render 3D.d: The camera and lighting engine that turns every 3D node into a real picture, physically-based Cook-Torrance/GGX materials, ACES tonemapping, and MSAA antialiasing, all live, with up to 4 geometry inputs plus camera, light, and HDRI.

Draw.d: A live paint canvas right inside the node graph, soft round, hard round, square, spray, chalk, and ink-bleed brushes, plus a dedicated eraser toggle.

Resynthesize.d: An iterative image mutator: instead of reprocessing the original source each frame, it feeds its own previous output back into itself and mutates it again, so the image drifts progressively further from the source over generations.

Fit.d: Resizes and reflows whatever image comes in to a target width and height, with a mode of Fit (letterbox), Fill (crop to fill), Stretch (ignore aspect ratio), or Native (pass through).

Comment.d: A plain annotation box, it does no image processing at all and produces no output. It just holds a block of text plus its own size and background color so you can label or explain parts of a patch.

Group.d: A resizable, colored backdrop for organizing the node editor, not a functional processing node, it has no output of its own. Any node sitting inside it gets dragged along when you move the group's header.

Null.d: A zero-cost reroute point: it simply reports whatever texture is plugged into it as its own output, without rendering anything itself. Meant purely for tidying up cable runs in a busy patch.

Viewport.d: Functionally identical to Null (a free pass-through, no processing) but drawn with a large canvas, so you can actually inspect the image at a given stage of a patch instead of judging it from a tiny thumbnail.

Curves.d: Draggable tone curves for the combined RGB channel plus red, green, and blue individually, the precise, hands-on way to push contrast or introduce a color cast exactly where you want it.

Color Ramp.d: Recolors any grayscale source by mapping its brightness onto a custom gradient with up to 32 stops, the classic trick for turning plain noise or a height map into something that looks painted.

Remove Background.d: Uses Apple's on-device Vision framework to cut a subject or person cleanly out of a live camera feed, no green screen required.

Feedback.d: Two related nodes that feed a frame back into itself with a slight zoom, spin, or fade, the same trick behind classic video-feedback tunnels. Every new stroke or shape leaves a trail that spirals off into infinity.

Trails.d: Two related nodes that feed a frame back into itself with a slight zoom, spin, or fade, the same trick behind classic video-feedback tunnels. Every new stroke or shape leaves a trail that spirals off into infinity.

Reaction Diffusion.d: Simulates the same Gray-Scott chemistry that grows animal spots, coral, and cellular patterns in nature, feed it a nudge and organic, living patterns spread and evolve on their own.

Blend.d: Combines two images with a wide range of blend modes, Multiply, Screen, Overlay, and more, plus an opacity dial. This is how you layer a glowing shape over live video, or double-expose two textures.

Layer Stack.d: A multi-layer compositor with per-layer blend mode, opacity, and visibility, think of it as a mini layers panel living inside your node graph, for building a full scene from separate pieces without a tangle of individual Blend nodes.

Switcher.d: Cycles automatically among up to 4 connected image inputs on a timed interval (beats or seconds, synced to the transport), with a crossfade control blending the outgoing and incoming input, or a manual toggle to freeze on one chosen slot.

Output.d: The last node in every patch, sends your visuals and audio to the screen and speakers, and can record both to disk at once as an H.264 movie, ready to share or edit further.

Syphon Out.d: Broadcasts whatever image, 3D render, or shader is plugged into it out to other Mac apps in real time, Resolume, OBS, TouchDesigner, MadMapper, via zero-copy GPU memory sharing, with a customizable server name.

NDI Out.d: Publishes the connected image as a named NDI video source on the local network for OBS, vMix or Resolume. Video only. Without the NDI runtime the node says so and everything else keeps working.

Projection.d: A projection-mapping and warping node for driving real projectors, 4-corner perspective warping or a subdivided mesh- grid warp, with built-in alignment test patterns for lining up a physical projector.

LFO.d: A slow, repeating wave, sine, triangle, saw up, saw down, square, or sample-and-hold, that you plug into almost any knob in the patch to make it move on its own, in time with the music if you like.

Random.d: Generates a new target value on a timer, then eases toward it using a smoothing amount, 0 for hard stepped changes, higher for a fully eased curve. Low/High rescale the range, and each node spawns with its own seed.

Pattern.d: A 16-step sequencer whose value steps through hand-set slots once per set beat length, looping back to the start, with a smoothing option to ease between adjacent steps instead of jumping.

Math.d: Combines two other modulator signals using one of ten operations, add, subtract, multiply, divide, min, max, average, and more, then scales and offsets the result.

Compare.d: Tests two modulator inputs against each other using >, >=, <, <=, ==, or != and outputs a hard 1 or 0, with a tolerance value for the equality checks.

Range to Range.d: Linearly remaps an input modulator from one span to a different output span, with an option to clamp the result inside the output bounds.

Smoothing.d: Runs an exponential moving average over an input modulator, with an amount knob setting the filter strength, taking the edge off a stepped or noisy source.

Invert.d: Mirrors an input modulator around a low/high pivot, so rises become falls and vice versa, and it still behaves correctly on signals that run outside the usual 0..1 range.

Mod Depth.d: Scales how much of an incoming modulator's swing reaches its destination with a single depth knob from -1 to 1, at 0 the signal has no effect, negative values invert it while still scaling.

Mod Curve.d: Reshapes an input modulator through a user-drawn transfer curve, with a mix knob blending between the raw input and the fully-curved result.

Drift.d: Learns where you leave each knob and how fast you move it, then keeps the knob going after you let go: it settles into your usual places and wanders between them at your pace.

Moves.d: Moves is a prediction node: it guesses where a value or a phrase goes next and drifts around that guess. It has no input and gives prediction out.

Predictive Modulator.d: Learns a small model of one modulator you patch in, then keeps that motion going on its own once learning stops. Draw a gesture once and it carries on in the same spirit.

Predictive Coloring.d: Learns what graded footage looks like to you and grades incoming frames toward it.

CV to Pitch.d: Quantizes a continuous modulation signal into semitone steps, optionally snapped onto a chosen scale and root, with a glide option for portamento smoothing on the stepped output.

Macro Knob.d: A single manually-set control meant to be performed rather than left alone, with a curve exponent to ease the response in or out and an invert switch.

Macro Slider.d: A plain 0-to-1 fader, the simplest possible performance control, meant to be grabbed and pushed rather than automated.

Macro Bipolar Knob.d: A center-detent knob that swings -1 to +1 rather than 0 to 1, so its resting position genuinely means "no effect", ideal for anything you want to push both directions from a neutral center, like a pan or a pitch bend.

Macro XY.d: A 2D performance pad, grab it with a mouse or trackpad to fling two parameters around at once, live. It can also record a path you drag out and loop it back for hands-free, repeating motion.

Macro Toggle.d: A latching on/off switch, plain and simple, click once to flip it on, click again to flip it off.

Macro Trigger.d: A momentary bang pad: it fires to 1 the instant you press it and drops back to 0 the instant you release, with its own flash so you can see exactly when it fired.

Macro NumBox.d: A draggable, typeable number box with its own min/max/step range, for a performance control where you want to see and dial in an exact value rather than eyeball a knob's position.

Macro Radio Selector.d: A discrete multi-choice selector, pick one of a set number of options and it outputs that choice's position, evenly spaced across 0 to 1.

Macro Step Gate.d: An 8-step rhythmic gate sequencer locked to the transport, toggle any of the 8 steps on or off and it outputs a 1-or-0 pulse in time with the beat, by default at sixteenth notes.

MIDI CC.d: MIDI Learn for a single physical control on your USB MIDI hardware, click Learn, twist the knob, and it remembers that device's exact channel and controller number.

MIDI Trigger.d: Turns a MIDI pad hit into a decaying envelope pulse (Pad mode, bound to one note), or reports whichever note was last played on the channel (Keyboard mode).

Path.d: Moves a point along a shape over time, Circle, Line, Figure Eight, Helix, Spiral, or Lissajous, outputting separate X, Y, Z, and progress channels, tempo-synced by default.

Geometry Table.d: Samples up to 16 points off a patched mesh and reports each one as its own X/Y/Z modulator, plus an overall centroid and spread, turning the literal shape of a piece of geometry into a bank of control voltages.

Constant.d: Outputs one fixed, unmoving value, exists because math-utility nodes only take other modulators as input, so this supplies a literal number.

Null Modulator.d: A zero-cost pass-through junction for a modulator cable, useful as a named point in a chain where you can read a live value meter or branch one signal to several destinations.

Image Analyze.d: The visual mirror of Audio Analyze, reads brightness, color channels, saturation, hue, motion, and where the action is happening on screen, turning all of it into modulation.

Palette.d: Extracts a small color palette from a reference image or live video, clustering colors in Oklab space with sort, chroma, and mood-shaping controls (hue shift, saturation, brightness).

Audio File.d: Loads and plays back an audio file independently of the live mic/line input, exposing the same analysis taps as live input so a backing track can drive visuals deterministically.

Audio Analyze.d: Listens to any audio and splits it into 8 frequency bands plus a transient onset trigger, the node that lets visuals genuinely react to music, band by band, hit by hit.

OSC Receive.d: Listens on a network port for OSC messages matching an address pattern and reports the last value received as a modulator, remapped to a low/high range, it patches in exactly like an LFO or Random node, just driven by another app or device instead.

OSC Send.d: The one node with no output at all: it reads whatever modulator is patched into it and sends its value out over the network as an OSC message, so a lighting console, Max/MSP patch, or another OSC-speaking app can react to what's happening inside Infinite.

Oscillator.d: A single-voice synth on the wavetable engine, offering four waveforms (Sine, Triangle, Saw, Square) with pitch, glide, pitch bend, and an audio-rate FM/PM input whose depth and mode you control directly.

Wavetable.d: Wavetable is a synth: it turns notes into sound. It takes notes and audio in and gives audio out. Its controls include mix  a-b, volume, freq, glide.

Analog.d: A polyphonic virtual-analog voice: two oscillators (the first a unison stack), a sub oscillator, noise, a drive stage, a nonlinear filter (Moog ladder, MS-20, diode ladder or SVF) and an amplitude envelope across up to 8 voices.

Wave Terrain.d: Turns any 2D image or video texture into a "terrain" surface and reads audio by tracing a closed orbit across it, Circle, Lissajous, Lemniscate, Spiral, or Scanline, with full unison, an amp envelope, and a multi-mode filter.

Equation Synth.d: A Desmos-style oscillator: type a formula like y = sin(x + a) and it renders that curve as an anti-aliased, polyphonic wavetable waveform, so turning knobs A through D actually reshapes the wave's math instead of just modulating a fixed one.

Spectral Synth.d: Reads an image as a spectrogram: it scans horizontally while each row of pixels defines the amplitude of one of a bank of up to 256 sine partials, so a picture's brightness pattern literally becomes the sound's harmonic content.

Metallic.d: Physically models how real metal and glass actually ring when struck, eight material presets from Steel and Bell Bronze to Glass/Crystal and Vibraphone Bar, a genuinely resonant, inharmonic decay rather than a synthetic approximation.

Sampler.d: Load a file or record incoming audio, then play it back one-shot or looping (forward, reversed, or ping-pong) with independent pitch, finetune, and varispeed, and two playback lanes, polyphonic (MIDI-driven) and monophonic (free- running).

Slicer.d: Chops a loaded or recorded sample into slices, either by onset detection or by a grid locked to the transport tempo, and maps them chromatically across the keyboard starting at middle C, the classic MPC/Simpler-style chop workflow.

PaulStretch.d: Stretches any audio file up to 1000 times longer without changing its pitch, turning a two-second vocal snippet into an hours-long, slowly shifting ambient texture.

Molder.d: An evolving sound-design tool: it decomposes a recorded sample into tracked harmonic partials plus residual noise, then Roll mutates a parameter genome and re-renders a new sample from that, each roll drifting further from the last, not from the original source.

Grain Molder.d: Slices audio into overlapping grains, measures each one's loudness, brightness, or a random tag, and re-orders them along a blend between the original chronological order and a fully metric-sorted arrangement, at full amount it turns any recording into a rising or falling contour.

Granular.d: A real-time granular synthesizer that shreds a loaded or recorded sample into micro-grains and re-stitches them, with grain length, density, scan speed/position (with freeze), and stochastic randomization on position, length, pitch, and pan.

Field Synth.d: A polyphonic synthesizer whose entire voice algorithm is a kernel you write yourself, run per-voice on the audio thread, your own oscillator, FM algorithm, or wavetable scheme as plain math instead of a fixed engine.

Field Effect.d: Runs a Field kernel once per audio sample as a custom effect you write yourself, declare a bit of state for a delay line or filter memory, declare a param for an automatic modulatable knob, and write the DSP math directly instead of hunting for the right built-in.

Field Graph.d: Field Graph is a utility node: it routes signals in and out of Infinite or sets up the canvas. It has no input and gives picture out. Its controls include trigger input.

Drum Sequencer.d: An 8-track, 8-step sequencer for your own samples, complete with swing groove, mutes, and solos, build a full beat without leaving the canvas, and tap any lane's trigger to drive visuals too.

Plugin.d: Loads any Audio Unit you already own, synth or effect, right into the graph, with its native interface and up to 32 of its parameters exposed for modulation like any other Infinite node.

Gain.d: A simple audio level control: one dB knob raises or lowers the volume of the signal running through it, with an inline meter showing the output level.

Audio Meter.d: A stereo level meter with separate left and right bars on a -60 to +3 dBFS scale.

Audio In.d: Taps the computer's live input device (microphone or line-in) and brings it into the patch, with a gain trim and its own input-level meter.

Audio Out.d: The terminal endpoint of an audio chain, takes exactly one audio input and sends it to the real output device, and can record straight to a file in WAV, FLAC, or MP3.

Mixer.d: The app's dedicated summing node, taking up to 8 input slots, each with its own gain, pan, and mute, plus a per-channel peak meter and an overall summed-output meter.

Splitter.d: The explicit fan-out point for audio: since an audio output can only feed one destination, Splitter takes one input and makes it available to up to 4 downstream consumers as a passthrough copy.

Blend Audio.d: A two-input crossfader with a single Blend control: 0 plays only input A, 1 plays only input B, and 0.5 gives an equal- power blend of both.

Audio Texture.d: Turns an incoming audio signal into an image, rendering either a live Waveform or a Spectrum (FFT) view into a GPU texture, with adjustable FFT window size and smoothing.

Audio Color Ramp.d: Splits incoming audio into up to 8 frequency bands and maps each one to a color, Intensity mode glows a stop brighter with its band's energy, Expansion widens it, and Spectrum paints a continuous FFT sweep across the palette.

MIDI Notes.d: The note source, reads live MIDI input and turns it into note events for the rest of the chain, with a channel selector, a transpose knob, a velocity scale, and an option to snap incoming notes to the global key/scale.

Keyboard.d: Keyboard is a note node: it makes, filters or changes notes before a synth plays them. It has no input and gives notes out. Its controls include octave, transpose, velocity, numpad.

Note Filter.d: A gate on which notes get through, combining a scale/key filter, a pitch range, and a percent chance, a note only passes if it clears all three checks.

Note Transpose.d: Shifts every note by a fixed number of semitones, with an option to snap the result to the global scale.

Pitch Bend.d: A live pitch-bend knob (±2 semitones) that adds into each note's continuous bend amount rather than re-triggering the note, so moving it while a note is held slides that note's pitch in real time.

Velocity Curve.d: Reshapes how hard you hit the keys maps to output velocity, using a single curve exponent, below 1 boosts soft hits, above 1 favors hard hits.

Gate.d: Controls how long each note rings out with a single hold-time knob. At 0 it's a passthrough; above 0 it ignores the real note-off and schedules its own fixed duration for every note.

Humanizer.d: Adds random imperfection to a note stream with two independent knobs: timing jitter (when a note actually fires) and velocity jitter (how hard it hits). Both default to off.

Quantizer.d: Snaps each note-on forward in time to the nearest grid line, never earlier than when the note actually arrived, at a chosen musical division.

Glide.d: Fills the gap between one played note and the next with a fast run of very short in-between notes, approximating a portamento slide since the note system has no continuous pitch to bend smoothly.

Vibrato.d: A simple free-running sine LFO with one control, rate in Hz, meant as a substitute for true per-note vibrato, since note events have no continuous pitch channel of their own.

Note Echo.d: Repeats every incoming note a set number of times, each repeat spaced further apart, getting quieter and optionally shifting in pitch. The original note always plays first unchanged.

Predictive Notes.d: Wire a note chain in and press Learn.

Predictive Quantize.d: A groove quantizer instead of a grid one.

Predictive Velocity.d: A learned dynamics curve instead of a hand-drawn one.

Predictive Rhythm.d: Works like Predictive Notes, but learns pitch as a distance from a root note instead of absolute pitches.

Note Router.d: The system's note fan-out node: one input split across four separate outputs, chosen by Round Robin, Random, Probability, or Chain mode. A note's matching note-off always replays to the same output it was sent to.

Note Merge.d: The note system's fan-in counterpart to Note Router: merges up to 4 note streams into one output in timestamp order, keeping each input's notes as independent voices so two sources playing the same pitch at once sound as two overlapping notes instead of colliding.

Note Switcher.d: The note-cable counterpart of the image and 3D Switcher, cycles between up to four connected note sources on a timed interval or a manual slot, so a synth downstream hears only whichever source is currently active.

Arpeggiator.d: Takes held notes and breaks them into a rhythmic, tempo-locked pattern, Up, Down, Up-Down, Random, As-Played, and a dozen more traversal modes, with 1 to 4 octaves of range.

Note Sequencer.d: A dedicated step sequencer for melody, up to 16 steps, each with its own note, velocity, and on/off toggle, plus a gate- length control for how long each step rings out.

Random Note Generator.d: A self-running generator that produces its own note stream via a bounded random walk, each new note is the previous note plus a small random offset, clamped and quantized to a chosen scale and root. No note input needed.

Chorder.d: Turns a single held note into a full chord, with adjustable chord size, a strum offset, humanized timing and velocity, and scale quantization so nothing plays a wrong note.

Note Stack.d: Layers up to 8 extra transposed copies on top of every note that passes through, with the original note always passing through underneath. Each voice has its own semitone offset and on/off switch.

Note Capturer.d: Records whatever note stream feeds it, with tempo-relative timing so it stays in sync even if the BPM changes, then loops that recording back on top of the live input, which always keeps passing through.

Bouncing Balls.d: A physics playground that turns bouncing balls into music, balls glide inside a container shape and fire a note, quantized to a musical scale, every time they hit a wall.

Note Strum.d: Takes a chord's simultaneous notes and spreads their onsets across time in ascending pitch order, like a strummed guitar, while keeping each note's original gate length intact.

Envelope.d: Applies a classic ADSR contour to a continuous modulation signal rather than a note trigger, the "gate" is derived from the input crossing a threshold rather than a note-on/off.

Note to CV.d: Converts an incoming note stream's pitch into a normalized control voltage, holding the last played note's pitch rather than falling back to zero on release, a pitch tracker, not a gate.

Velocity to CV.d: Turns the velocity of incoming notes into a 0 to 1 modulator, with an adjustable velocity range. Hit harder and the value goes higher.

CV Recorder.d: Records any modulator you patch in.

Audio to CV.d: An envelope/amplitude follower that converts a live audio signal into a modulation signal, with gain, attack/release smoothing, and a peak/RMS detection mode.

Gaussian Blur.d: Two separate blur nodes for smoothing an image out, soft focus, depth-of-field, or just taking the edge off something too sharp. Often used right before a Bloom to make the glow itself feel softer.

Box Blur.d: Two separate blur nodes for smoothing an image out, soft focus, depth-of-field, or just taking the edge off something too sharp. Often used right before a Bloom to make the glow itself feel softer.

Motion Blur.d: Streaks an image in one direction, mimicking a fast camera pan or a subject moving quicker than the shutter can freeze. Instant sense of speed.

Radial Blur.d: Blurs outward from a single focal point you can place anywhere on screen, the classic zoom-punch effect used to slam attention onto one spot.

Unsharp Mask.d: Sharpens the image by comparing it to a blurred version of itself and boosting the difference, controlled by Amount and Radius.

Twirl.d: Three separate optical-warp nodes: Twirl spins a vortex around a center point, Pinch/Punch magnifies or implodes like a lens, and Ripple sends concentric water rings out from a point.

Pinch Punch.d: Three separate optical-warp nodes: Twirl spins a vortex around a center point, Pinch/Punch magnifies or implodes like a lens, and Ripple sends concentric water rings out from a point.

Ripple.d: Three separate optical-warp nodes: Twirl spins a vortex around a center point, Pinch/Punch magnifies or implodes like a lens, and Ripple sends concentric water rings out from a point.

Pixelate.d: Blocks the image into large flat squares to create a chunky, mosaic look, sized by Block Size.

Add Noise.d: Sprinkles random per-pixel grain onto the image, with Amount controlling how strong the speckling is.

Vignette.d: Darkens the corners and edges around a center point, with Amount for strength and Radius/Softness for how far the darkening spreads.

Transform.d: Moves, scales, and rotates the whole image using Translate, Scale, and Rotation controls, leaving anything pushed outside the frame transparent.

Posterize.d: Reduces the image to a limited number of tonal steps per channel for a flat, poster-print look.

Threshold.d: Converts the image to pure black and white based on a brightness cutoff point.

Exposure.d: Brightens or darkens the whole image in stops, the same control a camera's exposure dial gives you.

Show Alpha.d: Shows the alpha channel as a plain greyscale picture: white is solid, black is transparent.

Opacity.d: Opacity is a compositing node: it layers, masks and routes pictures. It takes picture in and gives picture out. Its controls include opacity.

Set Alpha.d: Replaces the alpha channel outright with the brightness of a second image you patch in: a hand-drawn matte, a Shape, a Ramp, or another branch's Show Alpha.

Alpha Invert.d: Swaps transparent for solid and back, and leaves the colour alone. It is the invert-matte switch a key would otherwise need a second node to get.

Alpha From Luma.d: Builds a new alpha channel from the picture's own brightness, so a black background becomes see-through with nothing to key against. Invert flips which end is solid, for a white-on-black source.

Alpha Levels.d: The Levels remap, applied to the alpha channel only.

Premultiply.d: Converts between premultiplied alpha (colour already scaled by its own alpha) and straight alpha.

Bloom.d: Two related nodes that make bright areas glow and bleed light into their surroundings, the way a real camera lens does when it looks at something dazzling. One of the fastest ways to make flat visuals feel expensive.

Diffuse Glow.d: Two related nodes that make bright areas glow and bleed light into their surroundings, the way a real camera lens does when it looks at something dazzling. One of the fastest ways to make flat visuals feel expensive.

Glitch.d: Six flavors of broken-signal chaos, sliced frames, RGB channel splitting, scanlines, blocky corruption, waving distortion, and full datamosh. Dial it from a subtle VHS wobble to full digital meltdown.

Lens Distortion.d: Bulges or pinches the image like a camera lens and fringes the edges with color, controlled by Barrel curvature and Chromatic Aberration amount.

Displace.d: Pushes pixels sideways using either a second connected image as a displacement map or, with nothing plugged in, an animated wavy pattern.

Liquify.d: Warps the image with a smooth, flowing animated distortion like moving liquid, shaped by Amount, Scale, and Speed.

Symmetry.d: Mirrors one half of the image onto the other across a chosen axis and center point, with an option to flip the whole result.

Kaleidoscope.d: Slices the frame into mirrored wedges around a center point, instantly turning ordinary footage into a mandala.

Mirror Tile.d: Tiles the image and flips every other tile so the edges meet seamlessly, unlike a plain repeat. Tiles sets how many repeats you get.

Chroma Key.d: Removes a chosen key colour, green-screen or blue-screen style, matching it in a way that ignores brightness.

Luma Key.d: Keys out a range of brightness (Low to High) instead of a colour, with Softness at the edges and Invert to flip which range is kept. The show option previews the matte.

Crop.d: Trims the edges of the image by set Left/Right/Top/Bottom amounts, then either leaves the trimmed area transparent, zooms in to fill the frame, or fills it with a solid color.

Emboss.d: Turns the image into a raised, carved-relief look by comparing pixels on either side of a light direction, with Amount and Angle controlling depth and lighting.

Normal Map.d: Works out a tangent-space normal map by treating the picture's brightness as a height field. The output switch can also show the raw normals, the source height, or the steepness of the slope.

Convolve.d: Runs a custom 3×3 grid of numbers over every pixel and its neighbors, letting you dial in blur, sharpen, edge, or emboss-style looks from nine kernel values.

Lookup.d: A related color-remap node that reads a reference gradient/table image to redirect each pixel's color.

Halftone.d: Recreates the image using a grid of dots sized by brightness (like a newspaper print), with Scale controlling dot density.

Edge Sobel.d: Classic Sobel edge detection. It outputs how sharply the picture changes as greyscale lines, and Invert flips black and white.

Edge Outline.d: Finds edges from the brightness gradient and draws them as flat-colour outlines over the original picture. Thickness and Threshold control how bold and how many.

LUT.d: Applies a color lookup table to your image by wiring in a second texture as the LUT reference, the same underlying idea colorists use for film-stock emulation, driven from an image input rather than a loaded file.

Gradient Map.d: Recolors the image by mapping its brightness onto a custom two-color (or multi-stop) gradient.

Color Adjustments.d: Your all-in-one grading desk: brightness, contrast, levels, color balance, hue, saturation, vibrance, and a black-and-white switch, the same toolkit colorists use, chained together in one node.

Outer Glow.d: Adds a soft colored glow that blooms outward from the image's edges or transparency, with Amount for strength and Color for tint.

Color Overlay.d: Tints the whole image toward a single flat color, with Opacity controlling how strongly the tint replaces the original colors.

Drop Shadow.d: Casts a soft offset shadow of the image's silhouette behind it, with Offset X/Y for direction and distance and Opacity/Color for its look.

Audio Filter.d: A classic analog-style filter with 12 types on tap, low-pass and high-pass at 12/24/36 dB per octave, band-pass, notch, shelves, and peak, with an envelope follower for auto-wah and a sidechain input so another sound can sweep the cutoff for you.

EQ.d: A five-band studio equalizer with a live filter-response curve you can see and drag, carve out mud, add air, or fix a harsh frequency, watching the curve move as you turn each knob.

Dynamics.d: A compressor that squashes loud peaks down once they cross a Threshold, tightening dynamics by a set Ratio, with Attack/Release/Makeup rounding out the feel.

Limiter.d: A brick-wall ceiling that catches anything above the Threshold and prevents it from getting louder, with In/Out Gain to drive it harder or make up level.

Delay.d: A tempo-synced ping-pong delay with feedback, tone shaping, panning, and ducking, everything from a tight slapback to a rhythmic, bouncing echo.

Reverb.d: An algorithmic reverb with room size, decay time, damping, pre-delay, and stereo width, a wash big enough to sound like a cathedral, or small enough to feel like a tiled room.

Drive.d: Warm analog-style tube-and-transistor saturation with drive, bias, tone, and color controls, a gentle glow at low settings, real grit when you push it.

Stereo.d: Widens or narrows the stereo image with a Width knob (0 collapses to mono), plus Pan and a Bass Mono control that keeps low end centered.

Pitch Shifter.d: Shifts pitch up or down by semitones (up to two octaves either way) using a delay-line pitch shifter, with Grain size shaping the artifacts.

Chorus.d: Thickens the sound with multiple slightly detuned, delayed copies, with Delay time and Depth of the wobble and a free or tempo-synced Rate.

Flanger.d: Creates a sweeping, jet-plane whoosh by mixing a short modulating delay with Feedback back into the signal.

Phaser.d: Sweeps notches through the sound for a swirling effect, set by a Cutoff center frequency, Depth, and Rate.

Bitcrush.d: A separate lo-fi crusher: independent sample-rate (down to 200 Hz) and bit-depth (down to 1 bit) reduction for anything from a subtle vintage-sampler grit to full digital destruction.

Transient Shaper.d: Reshapes the punch of a sound by independently boosting or cutting the Attack (the initial hit) and the Sustain (the tail).

Stutter.d: Repeats a short slice of audio like a glitchy loop, with tempo-synced or free timing and a step/gate mask controlling which repeats play.

Ring Mod.d: Multiplies the signal by an oscillator to produce bell-like, metallic, robotic tones, with adjustable frequency and waveform.

Frequency Shifter.d: Shifts every frequency in the sound up or down by a fixed Hz amount (not musically, like pitch), creating inharmonic textures, with Feedback adding spiraling "barber pole" motion.

Tremolo.d: Pulses the volume up and down with an LFO, set by Depth and a free or tempo-synced Rate.

Formant Filter.d: Gives the sound a vowel-like, talking/singing quality by morphing between A-E-I-O-U formant shapes, with Q controlling resonance.

Wavetable Shaper.d: Distorts the sound by running it through a chosen wavetable, with Table picking the waveform set, Position scanning through it, and Drive controlling intensity.

Resonator Bank.d: Up to 16 band-pass resonators running side by side, forming a tuned bank of ringing filters, including a metallic tuning mode. Feed it noise or drums and it rings like a struck bell or plate.

Cycle Shaper.d: Distorts and crossfades the shape of a single waveform cycle. A way to bend a plain tone into harder, brighter, or stranger timbres.

Spec Blur.d: A streaming phase vocoder that smears the spectrum over time. Sharp hits dissolve into a harmonic cloud, with tilt, phase diffusion and freeze controls. It adds 42.7 ms of delay, and its mix defaults to fully wet.

Circle.d: Circle is a source node: it makes a picture from nothing, so it sits at the start of a visual chain. It has no input and gives picture out. Its controls include shape, width, height, size x.

Ellipse.d: A filled or stroked ellipse. Aspect stretches it away from a perfect circle, so one dial takes you from a dot to a wide lens shape.

Rectangle.d: A filled or stroked rectangle with an optional corner radius. The simplest building block for panels, bars, frames, and mattes.

Rounded Rect.d: A rectangle with rounded corners. It is the same as Rectangle, but the corner radius gets its own control so you can animate it directly.

Triangle.d: Triangle is a source node: it makes a picture from nothing, so it sits at the start of a visual chain. It has no input and gives picture out. Its controls include shape, width, height, size x.

Polygon.d: A regular polygon, and Sides sets how many. Three is a triangle, five a pentagon, and a high number slides toward a circle.

Star.d: Star is a source node: it makes a picture from nothing, so it sits at the start of a visual chain. It has no input and gives picture out. Its controls include shape, width, height, size x.

Ring.d: Ring is a source node: it makes a picture from nothing, so it sits at the start of a visual chain. It has no input and gives picture out. Its controls include shape, width, height, size x.

Line.d: Line is a source node: it makes a picture from nothing, so it sits at the start of a visual chain. It has no input and gives picture out. Its controls include shape, width, height, size x.

Hexagon.d: A six-sided regular polygon. It is a Polygon with Sides locked at six, for when you simply want honeycomb geometry with one less thing to dial in.

Arrow.d: Arrow is a source node: it makes a picture from nothing, so it sits at the start of a visual chain. It has no input and gives picture out. Its controls include shape, width, height, size x.

Crescent.d: A crescent-moon shape, made by subtracting one circle from another. Move the two circles apart and the crescent fattens or thins.

Gear.d: Gear is a source node: it makes a picture from nothing, so it sits at the start of a visual chain. It has no input and gives picture out. Its controls include shape, width, height, size x.

Superellipse.d: A squircle: a shape that lives between a rectangle and an ellipse. Inner Ratio tunes how square or how round it feels, the same silhouette you see on app icons.

Pie.d: A circular wedge. Inner Ratio controls how much of the circle is cut away.

Teardrop.d: A teardrop or droplet outline: round at the bottom, pointed at the top. Handy for water, ink, and leaf-like motifs.

Chevron.d: An angled bracket, or chevron. Stack and repeat it for arrows, speed lines, and rank badges.

Blob.d: An organic, wobbly rounded shape, randomised by seed-like controls rather than a precise geometric primitive.

Plane.d: Plane is a 3D node: it builds, changes or lights geometry that Render 3D turns into a picture. It takes picture in and gives 3D shape out. Its controls include shape, detail, sides, bevel.

Cube.d: Cube is a 3D node: it builds, changes or lights geometry that Render 3D turns into a picture. It takes picture in and gives 3D shape out. Its controls include shape, detail, sides, bevel.

Sphere.d: Sphere is a 3D node: it builds, changes or lights geometry that Render 3D turns into a picture. It takes picture in and gives 3D shape out. Its controls include shape, detail, sides, bevel.

Icosphere.d: Icosphere is a 3D node: it builds, changes or lights geometry that Render 3D turns into a picture. It takes picture in and gives 3D shape out. Its controls include shape, detail, sides, bevel.

Torus.d: Torus is a 3D node: it builds, changes or lights geometry that Render 3D turns into a picture. It takes picture in and gives 3D shape out. Its controls include shape, detail, sides, tube.

Cylinder.d: A cylinder. Sides sets how many-sided it is; low values give a prism.

Cone.d: A cone. Sides sets how many-sided it is.

Torus Knot.d: Torus Knot is a 3D node: it builds, changes or lights geometry that Render 3D turns into a picture. It takes picture in and gives 3D shape out. Its controls include shape, detail, sides, tube.

Capsule.d: A cylinder with half-sphere caps, like a pill. The tube control sets the radius of the caps and the body together.

Tube.d: A hollow cylinder. Its inner radius sets the thickness of the wall.

Pyramid.d: A pyramid. Sides sets how many sides the base has, so 4 is the classic square pyramid and larger numbers lean toward a cone.

Prism.d: A prism: a polygon extruded into a solid. Sides sets the polygon, so 3 is a triangular prism and 6 is a hex bar.

Helix.d: Helix is a 3D node: it builds, changes or lights geometry that Render 3D turns into a picture. It takes picture in and gives 3D shape out. Its controls include shape, detail, sides, wire.

Supershape.d: A shape built from the superformula. Depth, tooth depth and hub hole warp it into gear-like or organic silhouettes, from starfish to flowers to cogs.

Tetrahedron.d: A four-faced platonic solid: the simplest 3D shape that can enclose space, made of four triangles.

Octahedron.d: An eight-faced platonic solid: two pyramids joined at the base, like a diamond.

Dodecahedron.d: A twelve-faced platonic solid with pentagon faces. It is the rounder of the classic solids and reads almost like a ball.

Rounded Cube.d: A cube with soft edges and corners. Corner radius sets how rounded it gets, from sharp-edged to almost a sphere.

Mobius Strip.d: A twisted strip with one side and one edge. Width sets how wide the band is.

Klein Bottle.d: The classic bottle with no inside or outside. It is a closed surface that passes through itself, which makes it a striking thing to light and rotate.

Gear 3D.d: A 3D cogwheel. Depth sets the thickness, and tooth depth and hub hole shape the teeth and the centre bore. It carries the 3D suffix because the 2D Shape node already has its own Gear.

Star 3D.d: A 3D star extruded into a solid. Depth sets how thick it is, and inner ratio sets how deep the points cut in. It carries the 3D suffix because the 2D Shape node already has its own Star.

Disc.d: A flat filled circle mesh, as opposed to Cylinder, which has height.

Arrow 3D.d: A 3D arrow made of a shaft and an arrowhead. It carries the 3D suffix because the 2D Shape node already has its own Arrow.

Union.d: Union is a 3D node: it builds, changes or lights geometry that Render 3D turns into a picture. It takes 3D shape in and gives 3D shape out. Its controls include mode, material from input.

Intersect.d: Intersect is a 3D node: it builds, changes or lights geometry that Render 3D turns into a picture. It takes 3D shape in and gives 3D shape out. Its controls include mode, material from input.

Difference.d: Difference is a 3D node: it builds, changes or lights geometry that Render 3D turns into a picture. It takes 3D shape in and gives 3D shape out. Its controls include mode, material from input.

Mesh to Points.d: Samples a mesh's vertices as a point cloud, ready for Instance on Points or Metaballs.

Mesh to Edges.d: Samples points along a mesh's edges as a point cloud, for Instance on Points or Metaballs. A good way to trace the outline of a shape with beads.

Mesh to Faces.d: Samples the centre point of every face as a point cloud, for Instance on Points or Metaballs. One point per face, so the density follows the mesh.

Array.d: Array is a 3D node: it builds, changes or lights geometry that Render 3D turns into a picture. It takes 3D shape in and gives 3D shape out. Its controls include operation, count, offset x, offset y.

Subdivide.d: Subdivision surface. Each level roughly quadruples the triangle count, so higher levels get expensive fast. Smooth controls how much it rounds corners.

Solidify.d: Gives a flat or open surface real thickness, turning it into a solid shell. Keep original also keeps the source surface.

Extrude.d: Extrudes every face of the input mesh along its own normal by Distance, with Inset shrinking each face first.

Wireframe.d: Replaces solid faces with a thin tube along every edge, at the Thickness you choose. A solid becomes a cage.

Triangulate.d: Re-cuts the mesh into triangles. Jitter randomises how each face is split, giving a more organic, less uniform look.

Normals.d: Recomputes how the surface faces the light. Flat shade gives hard per-face edges instead of smooth shading, and flip reverses which way every face points.

Explode.d: Pushes every face outward from the mesh's centre along its own direction, by Amount, with a different amount per face set by Seed.

Twist.d: Twists the mesh around a chosen axis by Angle: the further a point is along the axis, the more it rotates.

Smooth.d: Smooth is a 3D node: it builds, changes or lights geometry that Render 3D turns into a picture. It takes 3D shape in and gives 3D shape out. Its controls include operation, strength, pre-subdivide, iterations.

Mirror.d: Mirror is a 3D node: it builds, changes or lights geometry that Render 3D turns into a picture. It takes 3D shape in and gives 3D shape out. Its controls include operation, keep original, axis, plane offset.

Screw.d: Sweeps a profile around an axis in a spiral. Steps sets the smoothness, Turns the number of revolutions, Rise per turn the pitch, and Radius pushes the sweep outward.

Select.d: Select is a 3D node: it builds, changes or lights geometry that Render 3D turns into a picture. It takes 3D shape in and gives 3D shape out. Its controls include operation, axis, mode, facing.

Delete Selected.d: Delete Selected is a 3D node: it builds, changes or lights geometry that Render 3D turns into a picture. It takes 3D shape in and gives 3D shape out. Its controls include operation, keep selected instead.

Transform Selected.d: Transform Selected is a 3D node: it builds, changes or lights geometry that Render 3D turns into a picture. It takes 3D shape in and gives 3D shape out. Its controls include operation, move x, move y, move z.

Extrude Selected.d: Extrude Selected is a 3D node: it builds, changes or lights geometry that Render 3D turns into a picture. It takes 3D shape in and gives 3D shape out. Its controls include operation, distance, inset.

Delete.d: Removes the faces marked by an upstream Select node (or the instances, when it sits after Instance on Points). Turn on keep selected instead to flip it: everything except the selection goes, and only the selection stays.

MPC.d: A 16-pad sample player in the spirit of an MPC.

Sketch.d: Draws an image from a JavaScript sketch you write in the node, with loops, arrays and recursion and a p5.js-style API (rect, circle, line, beginShape, push/pop, translate, rotate, text).

Sketch 3D.d: Builds 3D geometry from a JavaScript sketch: box, sphere, cylinder, cone, torus, tube and beginShape/vertex/endShape, moved with translate, rotate and scale.

Field Notes.d: A note node whose body is a Field script.

FM.d: A 4-operator FM synth: four sine operators wired by one of 11 algorithms, from a 4>3>2>1 stack to four carriers side by side.

String.d: A physically modelled string: every note is a waveguide string tuned exactly to its pitch, on a shared wooden body.

Partials.d: Playable resynthesis: a loaded sample is analysed once into tracked partials plus the noise they leave behind, then every note plays it back additively at the note's pitch.

Convolution Reverb.d: A reverb whose room you design: shape (room, hall, chamber, tunnel), size, material, distance, decay time and stereo spread.

Saturator.d: Three saturation stages, each with its own curve (tube, tape, diode, fold, rectify, crush) and amount.
